Field surveys of Queensland school mackerel in the central Great Barrier Reef indicate that sexually mature females attain a fork length of 48 cm [Lp = 48 cm] by the time they become reproductively active, a size substantially smaller than the ultimate fork length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] that large adults can achieve as they approach their maximum body size. This marked difference between the size at which females first mature and the maximum recorded length reflects a life-history strategy common among fast-growing scombrids, where individuals invest heavily in early reproduction while continuing somatic growth. Lepidophagous and piscivorous feeding habits likely fuel this rapid size increase. The ecological implications of such a strategy are notable, as the relatively small size at puberty may allow more individuals to contribute to the spawning stock before they are removed by predation or fishing pressure in nearshore waters.

Under controlled aquarium conditions maintained at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the embryonic development of this species proceeds rapidly, with the hatching event occurring approximately 5.5 days [ab = approximately 5.5 days] after fertilisation. The resulting yolk-sac larva, an endotrophic prolarva that relies on its endogenous reserves prior to the onset of exogenous feeding, emerges as a tiny, transparent organism with a wet weight at birth of only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minute initial mass represents a dramatic contrast with the adult body size and underscores the extreme ontogenetic trajectory that characterises pelagic teleosts such as Scomberomorus queenslandicus. The first feeding stage, marked by yolk-sac resorption and mouth opening, typically follows within several days, after which the free-swimming larva transitions to an exotrophic existence in the planktonic environment.

Reproductive output in Queensland school mackerel has been estimated through fecundity analyses of gravid females. At the same water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], which is typical of the spawning grounds in northern Australian coastal waters during the summer monsoon season, batch spawning occurs and each female may release approximately 4,100 eggs per batch [N_R_i = approximately 4,100 eggs per batch]. Over the course of a protracted spawning season that can extend for several months, the maximum reproductive rate for an individual female translates into a daily output of about 4,100 eggs per day [Ri = about 4,100 eggs per day]. This value aligns with estimates from congeneric species such as Scomberomorus brasiliensis and indicates the capacity of this species to sustain high recruitment under favourable environmental conditions.

A length–weight relationship derived from a large sample of individuals captured across the species range provides a basis for converting fork length to body mass. The estimated wet weight at puberty for a 48-cm female is approximately 1,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,000 grams], while the ultimate wet weight, corresponding to the asymptotic body mass of the largest recorded individuals at 100 cm fork length, is about 9,550 grams [Wwi = about 9,550 grams]. This tenfold increase in body mass after the onset of sexual maturation is typical of moderately sized scombrids and implies a significant ontogenetic shift in metabolic demands and trophic ecology as growing individuals consume larger prey items. The relationship also suggests that most of the lifetime biomass accumulation occurs after females have already begun to contribute to the spawning stock, a pattern that buffers population productivity against size-selective fishing.

Longevity estimates for Queensland school mackerel, derived from otolith increment analysis and capture-mark-recapture studies, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] at the typical water temperatures of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] encountered throughout its distribution. This moderate lifespan, comparable to that of other Scomberomorus species of similar body size, positions the species as an iteroparous adult that may spawn repeatedly over several consecutive seasons. Given the relatively rapid maturation and high fecundity documented, the population dynamics of this species are likely driven by variable recruitment success linked to interannual fluctuations in oceanographic conditions rather than by the survival of a few long-lived individuals. Only a small fraction of hatched larvae ever survive the pelagic larval phase and its associated high mortality risk to reach the juvenile stage.
